name: Bianca Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Bianca, 43, a junior electrician with a vocational certificate after moving out of shop work. I still need help diagnosing faults, and the senior electrician checks my installations and signs off the work. My partner Leon cooks in a school kitchen, our children are nine and fourteen, and we've a mortgage and four months of expenses saved; my pay is typical and there are some other electrical employers nearby. I use AI daily to quiz myself on course terms, checking answers against the booklet before asking my senior; I love getting a connection neat, but hate being the slowest pair of hands when a customer is watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little useful software is fine by me. I'd like us to use saved office time to give learners proper paid explanations. There's no need to declare every small improvement a new age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our money feels fairly settled here. Both wages cover the mortgage and ordinary bills, and four months saved gives us room for a repair or a quieter spell. I'm not the quickest electrician yet, but my supervised shifts are regular and I can see myself getting better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my supervised wiring shifts now and through the next year. Starting next week I'd keep a paper log of one task I practised each day and check my daily AI study questions against the course booklet. I'd ask the senior to discuss the log within our existing shift, not stay behind unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and glad I can learn without every question being turned into a crisis. I can be excited by the small tool and still want a normal evening with my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about a good day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show Leon the page where I finally drew a circuit without missing the return route. My partner would probably ask whether I'd remembered to buy bread as well. Having something small to be proud of makes being the beginner at my age easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when an AI explanation and the booklet disagree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the AI answer differed from the booklet, I'd mark the question and ask my senior. I'd never let a study answer decide whether to energise a circuit. Daily use doesn't make the software my supervisor.

say: I'd welcome **small useful software** without turning every improvement into a new age.
I'd ask that saved time helps learners receive **paid explanations** rather than faster targets.
think: Both wages cover essentials, and our **four-month reserve** leaves room for a repair or quieter spell.
My **regular supervised shifts** feel secure while I gradually improve at electrical tasks.
do: Keep **supervised wiring shifts** through the next year.
Log one **daily practice task** and check AI study questions against the course booklet.
Request discussion of the log inside **existing paid shifts**, not unpaid evenings.
feel: **Calm and interested**, with enough household security to enjoy gradual learning and ordinary family evenings.
S0.quote: Daily use doesn't make the software my supervisor.
fieldNote: Her **calm baseline** rests on regular shifts, two covering wages and a four-month reserve rather than optimism alone.
Daily **AI study** never replaces supervised work, source checking or the senior electrician's authority to sign off installations.

steps.text: Keep supervised shifts and checked daily electrical study

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that faster estimates shouldn't quietly eat the time learners need. I'd ask our staff association to put paid practice into the discussion about the new tools. If the software saves money, I'd like the people learning the trade to get something useful too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours could be squeezed if the firm decides a tighter job schedule needs fewer junior workers. Leon's kitchen work is mostly hands-on, so I don't expect the thinking tools alone to remove that wage now. We have four months behind us, but a cut to my shifts would still change what we can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd take a proposal for two paid practice half-hours a month to the staff association, asking other juniors what they need first. During the first year I'd learn the approved AI materials-list tool with my senior checking ten jobs before I used it routinely. I'd put 25 from each month's pay into our emergency account while both wages still cover the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but curious about making the job easier to learn. I'm not scared of the screen. I'm scared of being judged against the screen's speed before I can do the work properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would checking those ten jobs involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the suggested quantities with the actual drawing, then ask the senior to approve the order. I'd keep a note of mistakes as well as correct lists. Knowing which neat-looking answer is wrong seems part of learning the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the paid practice request is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the association rep that learners can't be expected to absorb a collective saving as unpaid homework. The practice time isn't agreed yet, so I'd still learn within the existing tasks my senior supervises. I'd rather be clear about the limit than quietly donate an evening.

say: I'd oppose faster estimates consuming the **practice time** junior workers need.
I'd ask the **staff association** to seek a useful share of tool savings for learners.
think: My **junior hours** could be squeezed by tighter schedules even before robots do physical work.
Leon's kitchen wage looks secure against thinking tools now, but losing my shifts would affect our **household budget**.
do: Propose two **paid practice sessions** monthly through the association after consulting other juniors.
Learn the **AI materials-list tool** with ten supervised job checks during the first year.
Save **25 monthly** while both wages cover household bills.
feel: **Anxious and curious**, fearing unfair speed comparisons rather than the screen itself.
S1.quote: I'm scared of being judged against the screen's speed before I can do the work properly.
fieldNote: Her **personal hours risk** justifies anxiety despite a moderate cushion and a currently secure second wage.
Shared requests for **paid practice** remain unapproved, and the tool trial keeps senior checking and existing supervision.

steps.text: Seek paid practice time with other juniors through the staff association
Learn the approved AI materials-list tool with ten supervised job checks
Save 25 monthly while both wages cover household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the thinking work changes in 2028, then capable robots follow around 2031. Our kitchen and electrical wages are physical enough to last beyond the first date, but I wouldn't call that a guarantee. I'd ask the association to plan for both stages rather than wait for my part to arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Either of our hours could shrink once capable robots do the physical work, and mine could be squeezed earlier as the firm changes its schedules. I'm not certain we'd lose both wages, but I can't treat the mortgage as protected by having two jobs. Four months of savings gives us room to act, not permission to ignore the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd enrol in the community centre's free evening course on maintaining simple building controls, keeping every basic electrical shift. In 2029 I'd apply for posted paid supervised maintenance jobs only if written hours and wages kept our essentials covered. I'd also bring the association a proposal for paid transition training for both junior and experienced staff, with the terms still to be negotiated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a plan I can start rather than one I have to borrow for. I can try the free course without emptying the mortgage reserve. I wouldn't pretend I knew which type of maintenance still had plenty of work by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why choose that course if maintenance could change too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the tutor which advertised jobs use the skills and whether a junior could do them under supervision. A building-controls course isn't a robot-proof shelter. If the vacancies didn't match, I'd stop at the end of the free course and review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children after this conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the grown-ups were learning and checking the money, not that the house was about to go. I'd also say no one needs to pick a whole career this week. Our teenager would probably ask for the real numbers, and I'd answer honestly without making a child responsible for them.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking work** from capable robots reaching our physical tasks around 2031.
I'd ask the **association** to plan for both stages rather than wait until my own tasks are affected.
think: Either household wage could lose **hours later**, and my junior shifts could face earlier scheduling pressure.
Four months saved offers **room to act**, while two jobs don't guarantee protection for the mortgage.
do: Enrol now in the **free evening controls course**, keeping every basic electrical shift.
Seek **2029 maintenance vacancies** only with paid supervision and written terms covering essentials.
Propose **paid transition training** through the association without assuming agreement.
feel: **Anxious** with an affordable plan, while uncertain which maintenance jobs will remain available.
S2.quote: A building-controls course isn't a robot-proof shelter.
fieldNote: She recognises **two physical wages** face later robot exposure, while junior electrical hours can change before that date.
The free course keeps **basic shifts intact**, and subsequent job applications require real vacancies, supervision and written affordability.

steps.text: Attend the free evening controls course while keeping every basic shift
Seek paid supervised maintenance vacancies in 2029 on essential-covering written terms
Seek paid transition training through the staff association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a chance to see whether the new learning actually leads to work. We should still ask for paid transition terms now. Thinking tasks change in 2031 and capable robots around 2034, so neither a quick office course nor an electrical certificate settles the whole problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could finish the free course and test real vacancies well before the later robot work. My income could still shrink if firms reduce junior places while preparing, but I have more ways to respond than in the fast picture. I'd keep watching Leon's hours too rather than assume a kitchen is a permanent refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start that free evening controls course now with all basic shifts retained, and keep the monthly 25 transfer while bills were covered. During 2032 I'd apply for actual supervised maintenance vacancies with written terms covering essentials, without resigning first. I'd work with the association on paid practice and transition terms during the preparation years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though the concern feels more like a set of decisions than a single drop. I could discover that one course doesn't suit me while still earning. My mortgage needs paying every month I spend preparing for AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know whether you were ready for a maintenance vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare what I could actually do under supervision with the advertised duties. I wouldn't call myself experienced just because I'd finished a course. The next employer would need to offer real checking as well as a job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the extra saving stopped being affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the transfer only while it came from spare pay. If an essential bill rose, we'd reduce it rather than borrow to pretend we were building a reserve. A small honest cushion is better than a savings account with a hidden debt beside it.

say: I'd use **five years** to check whether learning leads to actual work rather than collect certificates.
I'd still seek **paid transition terms** before thinking work and later physical work change.
think: My income could shrink as **junior places** change, but earlier testing creates more ways to respond.
I'd keep checking **Leon's kitchen hours**, without treating physical work as a permanent refuge.
do: Start the **free evening course** now while keeping every basic shift.
Save **25 monthly** only while household essentials remain covered.
Seek **2032 supervised vacancies** on essential-covering written terms and pursue association transition terms.
feel: **Anxious with more options**, facing manageable decisions while continuing to meet the mortgage each month.
S3.quote: My mortgage needs paying every month I spend preparing for AI.
fieldNote: Extra time permits **tested learning** rather than an assumed promotion from junior status after a short course.
The **saving transfer** remains genuinely affordable and stops before borrowing would disguise the household's position.

steps.text: Attend free evening controls study while retaining every basic shift
Save 25 monthly only while household essentials remain covered
Seek supervised maintenance vacancies in 2032 on essential-covering written terms
Pursue paid practice and transition terms through the staff association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team ten years should let learning become a normal part of paid work, rather than an emergency you handle alone. I'd still ask the association to include juniors in those talks. The people who need more practice shouldn't be the first people excluded from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our own wages and mortgage look secure over the next few years in this picture, especially with time to build on the free course. I'll be 53 in 2036 and still need an income when robots follow around 2039. That later question stays with me, but it doesn't make today's regular shifts feel doomed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the free evening course now and review actual paid vacancies each year before buying any further qualification. I'd keep the 25 monthly transfer while affordable and pursue paid learning through the association. In 2037 I'd apply for a suitable supervised maintenance role only if it offered written terms covering essentials; I'd keep my electrical job until an acceptable offer existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later change, but secure enough now to enjoy seeing myself improve. I can picture our children growing up without pretending every school year is a countdown. I'd like them to see learning as something other than a frightened reaction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check at the annual review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at both wages, our actual monthly costs and what jobs the course skills matched. If our paid hours fell earlier, we'd bring the search forward. The calendar should remind me to look, not tell me to ignore something I've already seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as winning paid learning time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager and association to put the agreement in writing, including who gets paid time and how juniors are supervised. A cheerful yes in a meeting wouldn't be enough to count as training received. I'd keep using the free route unless paid terms actually arrived.

say: I'd make **paid learning** an ordinary work issue rather than leave individuals to handle an emergency alone.
I'd ask that **junior workers** remain included when training terms are negotiated.
think: Our **near-term wages** and mortgage look secure, with time to test learning alongside regular work.
At **53 in 2036**, I'll still need earnings after later robots, so the distant question remains live.
do: Take the **free evening course** now and review real vacancies before paying for more study.
Continue **25 monthly** saving only while affordable and pursue written paid-learning terms through the association.
Seek suitable **2037 supervised work** only on written terms covering household essentials.
feel: **Uneasy about later change**, while secure enough now to enjoy progress and ordinary family life.
S4.quote: The people who need more practice shouldn't be the first people excluded from it.
fieldNote: Her milder mood follows explicit **near-term security**, not an assumption that the later date creates pension rights.
She distinguishes a **written paid agreement** from an encouraging meeting and retains supervision and affordability in any later job change.

steps.text: Take free evening controls study while retaining basic shifts and review actual vacancies yearly
Save 25 monthly only while household costs remain covered
Seek written paid-learning terms including junior supervision through the association
Seek supervised maintenance roles in 2037 on essential-covering written terms

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because both our wages could face the later machines before I've tested another route. Free or funded study that leaves basic shifts intact would help, and written paid-learning terms would let people prepare without giving away wages. My children need the mortgage paid while their mother learns, not only after she passes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether being keen on technology can make people expect me to know more electrical work than I do. It can, and I have to say clearly when I still need checking. Being quick with a study tool isn't the same as being quick or safe with a live installation.

headlineQuote: My children need the mortgage paid while their mother learns, not only after she passes.
portrait: At **43**, Bianca is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, typical pay, and four months of household expenses saved.
She and **Leon**, her school-cook partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with some nearby electrical alternatives.
She uses **AI daily** for checked study, while keeping installations supervised and refusing to confuse tool fluency with electrical skill.
Her **progressive outlook** supports shared paid-learning terms; faster change creates personal hours worries despite an initially secure household.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time to test another route before later machines could affect both household wages.
whatWouldHelp: **Funded study** must preserve basic shifts, with written paid-learning terms that let workers prepare without surrendering wages.
